## The idea

A printed score replaces some of the uncertainty of listening with visible
claims about pitch and duration. It does not remove interpretation. The useful
discipline is to preserve what the page says before deciding how Sonic Pi
should perform it. Keep a score-faithful event list in one layer and let a
renderer add synth choice, amplitude shaping, and articulation in another.

Measure and beat references give that event list a coordinate system. "The
third E sounds wrong" is hard to investigate; "measure 2, beat 3 differs from
the source" points directly to a comparison. Keep the source record from Lesson
42 nearby because the coordinate belongs to a particular edition. A pickup,
editorial division, or variant measure can change the numbering elsewhere.

Enter one voice and one bar at a time. Establish the time and key signatures,
then account for rhythm, pitch, ties, and articulation in that order. If a
printed note sounds strange beside a familiar recording, record the disagreement
instead of smoothing the score to match your expectation. Page and performance
are separate witnesses, and the transcription should say which one it follows.

## Run this

The event hashes use the book's shared `:note`, `:start`, and `:duration` keys,
with measure numbers attached as provenance. The first rendering follows the
data without shaping. The second derives amplitude and release from the same
events, so you can hear an interpretation without confusing it with a change
to the notated score.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

events = [
  {measure: 1, note: :c4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 1, note: :e4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 1, note: :g4, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :f4, start: 4.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :e4, start: 5.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :d4, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0},
  {measure: 2, note: :c4, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0}
]

define :play_events do |score, shaped|
  cursor = 0.0
  score.each_with_index do |event, index|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    phrase_amp = shaped ? 0.65 + (index * 0.05) : 0.8
    release = shaped ? event[:duration] * 0.82 : event[:duration]
    play event[:note], release: release, amp: phrase_amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep score.last[:duration]
end

play_events events, false
sleep 1
play_events events, true
```

Both statements attack the same pitches at the same times. In the second, each
successive note is a little louder and its release is shorter, creating a
gentle growth and narrow gaps. Those audible changes belong to the renderer.
The event list remains a checkable claim about what appears on the page.

## Change one thing

1. Shorten the G in measure 1 from 2.0 to 1.5. Measure 2 still begins at global
   start 4.0, so a half-beat hole opens before F. The silence identifies a
   damaged duration without shifting every later event.
2. Restore the G, then make the shaped amplitude formula subtract `index *
   0.04`. Only the interpreted rendering now recedes. Check the array afterward:
   no pitch, start, duration, measure, or source claim should have changed.
3. Add a `source_page` field either to every event or to a score object around
   the array. Print measure and page before each attack. Playback remains the
   same, while a disputed note becomes faster to locate on the original page.

## Why it works

The score layer behaves like immutable input. The renderer transforms that
input into timed Sonic Pi calls, but it does not rewrite the evidence it was
given. This separation lets several interpretations share one transcription.
It also lets duration and alignment checks run before reverb, synth envelopes,
or performance dynamics complicate what you hear.

Ties reveal why notation and sounding events are not always one-to-one. A tie
joins durations of the same pitch, producing one sustained sound rather than a
second attack. Encode the sounding event, then retain a comment or field that
describes the tie if later review needs the printed detail. A slur or phrase
mark usually changes articulation instead of event count, so it belongs in a
field that the renderer can interpret.

Accidentals require the scoped resolver from Lesson 40. Begin with the key
signature default, apply any accidental that governs the pitch within the bar,
then convert the resolved spelling to a Sonic Pi note or MIDI number. Reset the
bar-local accidental map at the bar line. A measure-by-measure representation
makes that scope visible and prevents an F-sharp from leaking into the next
measure because a mutable map was left uncleared.

When score and recording disagree, preserve both observations in separate
notes. A performer may alter rhythm, an edition may differ, or the recording
may use an ornament omitted from the page. The aim is not to force the witnesses
into agreement. It is to keep the source-faithful layer precise enough that an
interpretive renderer can depart from it knowingly.

## Take it further

Choose a short public-domain score from the inventory made in Lesson 42. Encode
at least eight measures of one voice with exact pitch, global start, and
duration. Attach source page and measure references, and annotate ties or
unclear print where they affect your decisions. Produce a score-strict
rendering and a performance-shaped rendering from the same array. Demonstrate
the separation by changing articulation, dynamics, or synth in the renderer
and confirming that the transcribed event data remains unchanged.
